content:
Two hadith reports appear again and again in lists of strange teachings in Islam: the one about a fly that falls into a drink, and the one about a woman told to nurse a grown man. Both are in the most trusted collections.

Their place in those collections is what gives the criticism its edge. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari or Sahih Muslim carries the highest grade of authenticity the hadith scholars give, so a Muslim cannot dismiss either one as a forgery. The question is what each report means, which kind of statement it is, and how the earliest Muslims applied it. Those questions have answers in the classical sources, and the answers are older than the modern objections.

The four points below set out a principle for reading such reports and then take each report in full, with what the Prophet's household and the jurists made of it.

Before taking any single report, it helps to know how Muslim scholars sorted the Prophet's words. When his advice on pollinating date palms produced a poor crop, he told the farmers that they knew better about their worldly affairs. Imam Muslim placed the report in a chapter on the duty to obey what the Prophet said as religion, as distinct from what he said on worldly matters by way of opinion.[1]

That distinction governs how the two reports below have been read. The first concerns household hygiene. The second concerns a single ruling of family law, which the Prophet's own wives treated as an exception.

Later scholars built a theory on that distinction. Shah Wali Allah of Delhi, writing in the eighteenth century, divided the reports of the Prophet into two kinds: what he conveyed as part of his mission, which binds the community, and what falls outside it, among which he listed medicine and the customs of his time.[2] Ibn Khaldun had made the same point about medicine four centuries earlier. The medicine handed down in the religious tradition, he wrote, is the medicine of the Bedouin of the time, and the Prophet was sent to teach the law, and medicine lay outside that mission; a Muslim may use such remedies for blessing, but nothing in them is part of revelation.[3]

The strongest form of the objection quotes the Quran: the Prophet does not speak from desire, and his speech is revelation revealed to him.[4] If every word he spoke is revelation, the argument runs, the distinction collapses. The commentators read those verses as a statement about the Quran he recited, which is their subject in the passage. The date-palm report shows the Prophet himself drawing the line, and the community has followed his lead.

Abu Hurayra reported that the Prophet said that if a housefly falls into a drink, one should dip it in and then remove it, because one of its wings carries a disease and the other its cure.[5] Al-Bukhari placed the report in the Book of the Beginning of Creation, under the heading of a fly falling into a drink.[5]

Critics treat the report as a medical claim and test it against modern microbiology. The text gives an instruction for a common situation in seventh-century Arabia, where drinks stood open and a fly in a cup was routine. Ibn Hajar, in his commentary on the report, calls the command to dip the fly an instruction of guidance (amr irshad), a counsel meant to set the remedy against the harm, and not an act of worship.[6] He also records a version, narrated by Abu Dawud and graded sound by Ibn Hibban, in which the fly shields itself with the wing that carries the disease, so that the wing carrying the cure is the one that goes in last, and he explains the word "disease" there as poison.[6] Nothing in the report obliges anyone to drink from a cup a fly has touched. Read through the principle above, a remark of this kind falls under worldly matters, where the Prophet himself told his companions that they knew best. A Muslim who pours the drink away breaks no rule of religion.

The report is well attested. Besides the chain from Abu Hurayra in al-Bukhari, it was narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, and it appears in the collections of Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah.[7] The objection to it is also old. In the twentieth century the Egyptian writer Mahmud Abu Rayya made it a centrepiece of his attack on Abu Hurayra and on the hadith literature as a whole, and scholars of his own country wrote replies.[8]

Some modern Muslim writers have gone the other way and cited laboratory studies of substances on the bodies of flies that act against bacteria. Those studies say nothing about dipping a fly in a drink, and the case for the report does not need them. The text gives a practical instruction for a situation that every household in Medina met, and pairs the harm with its remedy. Whether a reader takes the remedy as medicine, as encouragement not to waste a drink, or as a worldly remark of the kind the Prophet distinguished from religion, no ruling of the law depends on it, and the jurists drew none from it beyond the purity of the drink.[6]

Sahla bint Suhayl told the Prophet that her husband Abu Hudhayfa was unhappy when Salim, Abu Hudhayfa's client (mawla, a freed dependant attached to his household), came into their home. Salim was by then a grown man who had fought at Badr. The Prophet told her to nurse him so that he would become her foster son and unlawful to her in marriage. She asked how, since he was a grown man, and the Prophet smiled and said that he knew it.[9] She later reported that she did so and that the unease in Abu Hudhayfa's heart went away.[10]

The context is the Quran's command to call adopted sons by the names of their own fathers, which ended adoption as a legal tie of kinship.[11] The ruling gave Salim, who had long been part of the household, a lawful family bond with Sahla. The report does not say how the milk was given, and a narrator in the chain, Ibn Abi Mulayka, said that he held back from narrating it for about a year out of caution.[12]

The commentators addressed the question that occurs to every modern reader. Al-Nawawi, in his commentary on Sahih Muslim, quotes Qadi Iyad: Sahla probably drew the milk and gave it to Salim to drink, without his touching her or seeing what he was not permitted to see, since that would not be lawful.[13] The jurists who discussed fosterage in general had already defined it as milk reaching the stomach of the child, by any route, so the report needs no physical contact to make sense.

The strongest form of the criticism says that the ruling is degrading whatever its method. The reader should keep in view what the ruling was for. Adoption had just been abolished as a legal tie, and a young man who had grown up as a son in the house suddenly became a stranger in law to the woman who had raised him. Sahla came to the Prophet with a real problem in her own household, and the answer gave Salim a lawful place in it.

Umm Salama reported that the other wives of the Prophet refused to let anyone enter their homes on the basis of such fostering, and told A'isha that they regarded it as a concession the Prophet had given to Salim alone.[14] A'isha herself narrated the general rule that fosterage arises only from hunger, that is, in infancy, when milk is a child's food. Al-Bukhari placed that report under the heading that there is no fosterage after two years.[15]

The household was divided, and the sources say so. A'isha herself applied the Sahla ruling more widely. Malik records in his Muwatta that when she wanted a man to be able to visit her, she would ask her sister Umm Kulthum or her brother's daughters to nurse him, and that the other wives refused to follow her, holding it to be a concession for Salim alone.[16] A'isha also narrated the general rule about hunger, and the jurists had to weigh her practice against her report.

Most of them weighed it the way the other wives did. The four Sunni schools hold that fosterage which creates family ties takes place within the first two years of life, on the basis of 2:233 and the report on hunger. A minority took a different view: al-Layth ibn Sa'd and Ibn Hazm held that nursing an adult creates the tie, and Ibn Taymiyya held that it does so where there is a real need of the kind Sahla faced.[17] Even that minority treated the ruling as a narrow remedy for a household problem.

The Quran sets the full period of nursing at two years.[18] Read with A'isha's report on hunger, that limit became the basis on which jurists held that nursing an adult creates no family tie. Critics who present the Sahla report as a general Islamic practice are describing a position that most of the Prophet's own household rejected, and that the four schools of law set aside.

The bottom line

Both reports are authentic, and neither means what the lists of strange teachings make of it. The fly report gives a household instruction from a time when flies in open cups were a daily matter, and Muslim scholars from Ibn Khaldun to Shah Wali Allah set such instructions apart from the law the Prophet was sent to teach. The Sahla report records a single ruling for a household left in difficulty by the end of adoption, which the Prophet's wives argued over, and which the schools of law confined to Salim or to cases of the same kind.

A reader who meets either report in a list should ask what kind of statement it is, who applied it and how. Those are the questions the scholars of hadith asked first, and the answers are in the commentaries the critics rarely quote.

  2. Shah Wali Allah al-Dihlawi, Hujjat Allah al-Baligha, chapter on the two kinds of knowledge conveyed from the Prophet.
  3. Ibn Khaldun, The Muqaddimah, trans. Franz Rosenthal, chapter 6, section on medicine.
  4. Quran 53:3–4.
  5. Sahih al-Bukhari 3320, Book of the Beginning of Creation, chapter on a fly falling into a drink, report of Abu Hurayra.
  6. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari, Salafiyya edition, vol. 10, pp. 250–251 (Shamela text), commentary on Sahih al-Bukhari 5782, the chapter on a fly falling into a vessel.
  7. Sunan Abi Dawud 3844 (from Abu Hurayra); Sunan al-Nasa'i 4262 and Sunan Ibn Majah 3504 (from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri).
  8. Mahmud Abu Rayya, Adwa ala al-Sunna al-Muhammadiyya (Cairo, 1958); among the replies, Mustafa al-Siba'i, al-Sunna wa Makanatuha fi al-Tashri al-Islami.

  10. Sahih Muslim 1453b, ibid.
  11. Quran 33:4–5.

  14. Sahih Muslim 1454, ibid., report of Umm Salama.
  15. Sahih al-Bukhari 5102, Book of Marriage, chapter that there is no suckling after two years, report of A'isha.
  16. Malik ibn Anas, al-Muwatta, Book of Suckling, chapter on the suckling of an adult.

  18. Quran 2:233.
